nameStory: The Lake Darner gets its name from its strong preference for larger bodies of water, particularly lakes and ponds. Unlike many of its relatives that patrol streams or smaller wetlands, this dragonfly is most at home cruising over the open waters of New England's lakes. The term 'darner' comes from the old belief that dragonflies could sew up your lips or ears with their needle-like bodies!
description: The Lake Darner is a large, powerful dragonfly that patrols New England's lakes and ponds with impressive speed and agility. These substantial insects have the typical darner build - a long, slender body and broad, clear wings that can span nearly four inches. Their bodies display the classic dragonfly colors of blues and greens with intricate patterns, making them one of our more striking aerial predators. Like all dragonflies, they're voracious hunters that spend most of their time on the wing, snatching mosquitoes and other small flying insects from the air.

idTips.label: Black facial line
idTips.description: Look for a distinctive black line running across the face between the compound eyes - this dark stripe is like a superhero mask and is the Lake Darner's signature feature that separates it from similar species

idTips.label: Large size
idTips.description: These are hefty dragonflies that feel substantial if you cup one gently in your hands - they're among the bigger darners you'll encounter in New England

idTips.label: Blue and green coloration
idTips.description: The body shows beautiful blue and green markings that can shift and shimmer in sunlight, with the colors appearing most vibrant on fresh individuals

idTips.label: Lake habitat preference
idTips.description: Unlike stream-loving darners, these patrol open water areas where you can watch them make long, straight flight paths back and forth across the lake surface

idTips.label: Clear wings
idTips.description: The four wings are transparently clear with just a hint of shimmer, and you can hear them make a crisp rustling sound during flight

habitat: Lake Darners are found around larger bodies of water throughout New England, particularly natural lakes, large ponds, and quiet backwaters of rivers. They prefer areas with some emergent vegetation like cattails or sedges around the edges, but spend most of their time patrolling over open water rather than hovering near shore. You're most likely to spot them at lakes in forested areas, from low elevations up into the mountains.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from their aquatic larval stage in late spring, but they're not yet at peak numbers. Early individuals may be seen patrolling larger ponds and lakes.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight season when Lake Darners are most active and easiest to spot. They patrol territories over open water during warm, sunny days and are most active from mid-morning through late afternoon.
seasonality.fall: Numbers decline through early fall, though some individuals may persist into September. Mated females can be seen laying eggs by dipping their abdomens into the water near vegetation.
seasonality.winter: Adults are gone, but the aquatic larvae (nymphs) continue developing underwater beneath the ice, where they'll spend one to several years before emerging as adults.

funFact: Lake Darner larvae are underwater dragons that can live for several years as aquatic predators before transforming into flying adults - and they hunt by shooting out an extendable lower lip called a labium that unfolds like a spring-loaded grabber arm to snatch prey!
confusionNotes: Lake Darners are easily confused with Canada Darners, which are similar in size and overall coloration. The key difference is that distinctive black line across the Lake Darner's face - think 'Lake = Line' to remember this species has the facial stripe while Canada Darners have a plain face.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'eremita' means 'hermit,' which might seem odd for a dragonfly, but it likely refers to this species' preference for more remote, wilder lakes rather than urban ponds. This can make them trickier to observe than some of their more adaptable darner relatives.
compareHints: Among its Aeshna relatives in New England, the Lake Darner is most similar to the Canada Darner but distinguished by that black facial line. It differs from Shadow Darners by preferring open lake habitats over shaded woodland streams, and from Green-striped Darners by its larger size and different flight patterns. The facial marking is really your best bet for a confident identification when you can get close enough to see it clearly.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Aeshna relatives, the Shadow Darner stands out for its darker, more subdued coloration compared to species like the Green-striped Darner or Canada Darner, which show brighter blue and green markings.
Among its darner relatives, the black wing tips make this species fairly distinctive.
Among its Aeshna relatives, the Canada Darner is most easily separated by its northern distribution and association with cooler, forested waters.
Among its Aeshna relatives in New England, the lance-tipped darner's male abdominal appendages are uniquely sharp and spear-like, while species like the Canada Darner have more rounded or blunt tips.

Among its darner relatives, the Green-striped Darner is the only one with such vivid green thoracic stripes - Canada Darners have blue markings, Shadow Darners are much darker overall, and Variable Darners have more mottled patterns.
Among its Aeshna relatives in New England, the Variable Darner stands out with its broken thorax stripes - most other darners in this genus have more continuous stripe patterns.

Among New England's darners, the mottled darner stands out for its irregular, camouflaged patterning rather than the distinct stripes of the Canada Darner or the darker, more uniform coloration of the Shadow Darner.
